column4: The section's two-sided definition of divine testing is stated exactly here: God tests with both harm and good, so neither condition by itself is a verdict of honor.
Israel is tested with both good things and bad things so that they may return; this is the section's cited model for reading changing provision as تربِّي rather than rank.
Solomon calls an extraordinary gift فضل ربي ليبلوني and asks whether he will be grateful; abundance is consciously received as a test rather than proof of personal worth.
The garden owners are tested through a productive estate, joining the section's prosperous trial to a scene in which the recipients soon fail the needy.
The owners resolve that no poor person shall enter the garden that day; this is the concrete withholding exposed by the prosperity-test begun at 68:17.
God tests communities فيما آتاكم and immediately commands a race in good deeds; it joins the section's gift-as-test with its dictionary image of competing in generosity.
God raises people in differing degrees ليبلوكم في ما آتاكم; unequal gifts are examination material, not a scale of inherent honor.
Abundant water is promised in the hypothetical scene of steadfastness; 72:17 then identifies that very abundance as the medium of a test.
لنفتنهم فيه makes the plentiful water of 72:16 a trial within provision, directly blocking the inference that ample supply equals divine rank.
Wealth and children are explicitly فتنة, turning the family prosperity heard in 89:15 into responsibility rather than certification.
The repeated declaration that wealth and children are only a trial directly corrects the human reading of being enriched and indulged as honor.
After relief, the person claims the favor came through personal knowledge; بَلْ هِيَ فِتْنَةٌ gives the same correction as the section: the gift is a test.
Worldly splendor is something God uses to test groups, while رزق ربك is better and more lasting; visible luxury therefore cannot be the section's imagined rank.
The question names wealth and sons as what God keeps extending to some people, exactly the family abundance the human of the section mistakes for approval.
The answer rejects the inference that extended wealth and sons mean God is hastening good for them; this is a direct correction of ربي أكرمن.
ما غرك بربك الكريم addresses a person deceived about his generous Lord; it tightly links رب and كريم while exposing the same misuse of divine generosity.
ربائبكم اللاتي في حجوركم places stepdaughters and laps together, making explicit the foster-child household scene the section hears in رب and the dictionary sense of حجر.
Mary's Lord gives her a good growth, entrusts her to Zechariah, and supplies unexpected رزق; divine nurture, human guardianship, and provision meet in one child-care scene.
أكرمي مثواه is an instruction to honor the displaced child Joseph in the household, with the hope of taking him as a son; ikram is enacted care, not a status he boasts of.
The grown child must treat aged parents with إحسان and قولاً كريماً; the care once received returns as concrete honorable treatment.
The prayer كما ربياني صغيرا explicitly recalls parents raising the speaker when small and asks the Lord to repay that nurture with mercy.
Pharaoh claims ألم نربك فينا وليدا, invoking household upbringing as a debt; it supplies the section's child-raised-under-authority scene while questioning ownership of that care.
The infant Moses is placed under God's bestowed love and fashioned تحت عيني; divine care operates through a precarious foster setting before the child can protect himself.
Moses is returned to his mother, passes through repeated trials فتونا, and arrives at a measured time; nurturing and testing unfold as one long process.
Pharaoh's wife protects the found infant and proposes taking him as a son, a direct household reversal from exposed child to cherished child.
God restores Moses to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may not grieve; the child's shelter is shown as divine care delivered through restored family embrace.
Nursing, the father's duty of food and clothing, consultation, and protection from parental harm spell out the material work hidden inside the section's image of a child raised in care.
A mother's weakness upon weakness and two years of weaning make parental nurture concrete, and gratitude to God is paired with gratitude to the parents who carried it.
Pregnancy, birth, nursing, and mature gratitude form a full arc from received care to the adult's prayer for parents and descendants.
Housing, pregnancy support, and payment for nursing require continued care even after separation; it supplies the family obligation that 65:7 scales to the giver's means.
The person whose provision is restricted must still spend from what God gave him; constriction is neither humiliation nor release from caring for another.
God expands provision and measures it narrowly, while people rejoice in the nearer life; the verse separates fluctuating رزق from enduring value.
Kin, the poor, and the traveler are assigned a due before the passage names the Lord's expansion and restriction of provision at 17:30.
Even when one must turn away while awaiting provision, one must speak gently to the claimant; lack of means does not authorize humiliation.
The Lord both expands رزق and restricts it, placing the giving duties of 17:26-29 under divine apportionment rather than a verdict on worth.
After Qarun is swallowed up, yesterday's admirers finally say that God expands provision and restricts it; the collapse corrects their reading of wealth as honor.
God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it narrowly; the repeated formula directly matches فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ without calling the latter disgrace.
The alternation between expanded and restricted provision is offered as a sign, not a ranking of the recipients.
Immediately after the provision formula, the recipient is told to give kin, poor, and traveler their due; provision is read by what one does with it.
The Prophet is told to answer affluent deniers that his Lord expands provision and restricts it; their abundance does not validate their claim of immunity.
The same expansion-and-restriction formula is joined to God's replacement of whatever one spends, making generosity the response to provision in either measure.
After the claimant's wealth fails him, the passage asks whether people know that God expands and restricts provision; this supplies the lesson of 39:49 in explicit terms.
Ownership of the heavens' and earth's stores accompanies the statement that God expands and restricts رزق; the determining authority is the Provider, not social standing.
The verse explains that unrestricted abundance could make servants transgress, so God sends provision in a measure; restriction can itself be calibrated care.
God says even the unbeliever will receive temporary provision before judgment, proving that worldly supply cannot by itself mean divine honor.
God extends عطآء ربك to both seekers of this world and seekers of the next; receiving from the Lord is universal examination material rather than exclusive approval.
Worldly differences in فضل are visible, but the next life's degrees are greater; the verse prevents present provision from becoming the final hierarchy.
The call to lend God a good loan is paired with God contracting and expanding; generosity is required under the same sovereign variation the section describes.
God finds the Prophet an orphan and gives shelter; this is the section's decisive pattern of the child without a father receiving a new protective embrace.
God finds the Prophet in need and enriches him, setting received provision immediately before duties toward the orphan and petitioner.
Because the addressee was sheltered as an orphan, he is commanded not to overpower the orphan; received care must become care.
The petitioner must not be rebuffed, extending the anti-humiliation command from the orphan to another dependent person at the door.
The Lord's نعمة is to be voiced after the commands concerning orphan and petitioner; blessing is acknowledged through responsible remembrance, not private rank.
The denier violently repels the orphan, the clearest opposite of honoring and gathering the fatherless child into care.
Failure even to urge feeding the poor accompanies repelling the orphan, showing neglect as a social habit rather than a lack of private sentiment.
Birr includes giving loved wealth to orphans and other dependents, so true righteousness and honor are measured by transferred benefit rather than possession.
When asked what to spend, the answer expressly includes parents, kin, orphans, poor, and traveler; the cared-for person is turned toward a widening circle of care.
Concerning orphans, إصلاح لهم is best and living together is framed as brotherhood; the verse replaces neglect with accountable household inclusion.
Guardians must hand over orphan property and must not absorb it into their own; honoring the child includes preserving what is his.
Fear of failing justice toward orphans constrains adult household choices, making the vulnerable child's right the measure of the guardian.
Within the orphan-property passage, wards not ready to manage capital must still be fed, clothed, and addressed kindly; protective delay cannot become neglect.
Guardians test orphans until maturity, then release their property without haste or exploitation; trial here serves growth into competence, not humiliation.
When orphans and other dependents attend an estate division, they are to receive provision and kind speech; inheritance becomes a moment of active inclusion.
Guardians are told to imagine leaving their own weak children behind and therefore act justly; parental feeling is made the bridge to another child's protection.
Worship of God is immediately joined to إحسان toward parents, orphans, and the needy; relation to the Lord is verified by how dependents are treated.
The ruling exposes withheld entitlements of orphan women and commands justice for orphans, matching the section's sense of goodness delayed through disregard.
An orphan's property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity; absence of the father increases the guardian's duty rather than his license.
A fixed share of communal gains is assigned to orphans and other dependents, turning honor into an institutional allocation rather than optional feeling.
The orphan's property is protected until maturity and the covenant must be fulfilled; care continues over time when the child lacks a father's defense.
A wall preserves a righteous father's treasure for two orphan boys until maturity; providential delay protects their good, reversing the neglectful delay named in the section's dictionary note.
Orphans receive a designated share so that wealth does not circulate only among the rich; the verse directly overturns possession as social honor.
The righteous feed an orphan and other helpless people with food they themselves love; ikram appears as costly action directed outward.
The feeders seek neither repayment nor thanks, distinguishing care of the vulnerable from a generosity contest performed for personal rank.
Feeding is located on a day of severe hunger, so constrained conditions become the setting for generosity rather than an excuse to withhold it.
The recipient in that famine scene is an orphan of near kin, joining lost family protection to concrete food and renewed kinship.
أكرمكم عند الله أتقاكم supplies the measure the section says the prosperous person gets wrong: honor before God rests on taqwa, not abundance.
God honors all children of Adam and provides them with good things; human dignity precedes differing shares of wealth and cannot be inferred from their size.
The people of taqwa spend in ease and hardship alike; the two conditions of the section become two occasions for the same generous act.
Those who give remain fearful because they will return to their Lord; giving is not converted into a boast of assured rank.
These givers race in good deeds and reach them first, closely realizing the section's dictionary picture of a contest in generosity.
People of فضل and ample means are forbidden to stop supporting relatives and the poor after an injury; possessed favor must become pardoning, continued favor.
The Helpers prefer others even while having privation themselves, showing that restricted means can disclose honor through generosity.
When harm touches the ordinary human being he panics; it is one half of the unstable response to changing conditions that the section diagnoses.
When good touches him he withholds, directly connecting prosperity to the failure to pass care onward.
The exception is those whose wealth contains a recognized right, making ownership carry an obligation rather than a rank.
That recognized right belongs to the petitioner and the deprived, the very people whom self-reading prosperity tends to overlook.
The people who reserve that share are finally في جنات مكرمون; real honor follows faithful obligations rather than merely receiving wealth.
The generous person who gives and practices taqwa begins the path of ease, joining giving to the very criterion of honor in 49:13.
The opposite person is miserly and deems himself self-sufficient; perceived independence turns received abundance into withheld care.
His wealth cannot avail when he falls, exposing the false security on which the miser's self-ranking rested.
The أتقى person is kept from the fire, linking the Quran's highest piety term to the giver described in the next verse.
He gives his wealth to purify himself; the possession becomes a means of moral growth only when passed onward.
When mercy is removed after being tasted, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful; constriction is immediately misread just as in ربي أهانن.
When favor follows hardship, the human turns exultant and boastful; expansion is misread just as in ربي أكرمن.
Favor makes the human turn away arrogantly, while harm makes him despair, compressing the section's two mistaken readings into one verse.
The human never tires of asking for good but despairs when harm touches him, revealing attachment to condition rather than trust in the Giver.
Mercy after adversity prompts the claim هذا لي and imagined entitlement in the next life; granted relief is converted into personal rank.
The human transgresses precisely at the point where divine creation and generosity should have produced gratitude.
أن رآه استغنى identifies seeing oneself as self-sufficient as the cause of transgression, the inner error behind hoarding divine care.
People will be questioned about النعيم, turning enjoyed ease from a badge of honor into an accountable trust.
Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; material giving without honoring the recipient fails the section's outward meaning of ikram.
Misers conceal what God gave from His فضل and teach others miserliness; the response to divine bounty ends in a humiliating punishment, reversing their imagined standing.
Those called to spend may be stingy, but their stinginess is against themselves while God is rich and they are poor; dependence cannot be hidden by possession.
Those who spend before victory receive a higher degree than later spenders; Quranic rank is attached to timely generosity, not simply to having resources.
The command to spend is paired with deliverance from one's own greed; the decisive test of provision occurs in the act of releasing it.
Abraham's visitors are called ضيف إبراهيم المكرمين, introducing an honored-guest scene in which honor is immediately enacted as feeding.
Abraham quietly goes to his household and brings a fat calf, supplying the costly deed behind the guests' description as honored.
He brings the food near and invites them to eat; ikram is proximity, provision, and service offered to another.
The garden owner says he has more wealth and a stronger following, explicitly converting provision into a claim of superior rank.
His produce is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, collapsing the status claim of 18:34 and exposing wealth's contingency.
Qarun's vast stores lead to exultation, beginning the Quran's fullest scene of abundance being mistaken for personal distinction.
Qarun is told to seek the next life, do good as God did good to him, and avoid corruption; received favor is expressly redirected into outward good.
Qarun says he received wealth because of knowledge he possesses, the same self-attribution corrected as فتنة in 39:49.
Those desiring worldly life wish for Qarun's share when he appears in splendor, displaying the spectators' false equation of wealth with honor.
People of knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faith and good work, supplying the correct scale before Qarun's fall.
The earth swallows Qarun and no faction can help him, physically erasing the social height inferred from his provision.
The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished, directly voicing the inference rejected in the section.
Wealth and children do not bring anyone near to God; faith and good action do, replacing possession with accountable conduct as the measure.
God says worldly unbelief could have been accompanied by houses with silver roofs, showing that luxury is too indiscriminate to certify honor.
Silver stairways, doors, and couches continue the deliberately extravagant counterexample begun at 43:33.
Gold adornment is declared merely the enjoyment of worldly life, while the next life belongs with the Lord to the people of taqwa.
ومن يهن الله فما له من مكرم gives the true boundary of humiliation and honor: neither abundant nor restricted رزق lets a human assign God's verdict.
The condemned person is told mockingly that he is العزيز الكريم; the irony strips worldly self-importance of any claim to genuine karam.
Moses answers Pharaoh's claimed upbringing by pointing to Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; care used as leverage is exposed as a compromised نعمة.
Pharaoh calls Moses مهين while boasting of his own kingdom and bracelets; it exemplifies humiliation issued by a contemptuous ruler on the basis of visible status.
The hypocrites plan to stop spending so the Prophet's companions will disperse, using control of provision as an instrument of abasement.
Their boast that the mightier will expel the lowlier is reversed by the declaration that true might belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers.
A father receives news of a daughter with a darkened face, treating the arrival of a dependent child as damage to his own standing.
He considers keeping her على هون or burying her, the stark reversal of taking a vulnerable child into a nurturing embrace.
The buried girl is brought forward as the questioned party, restoring voice and standing to the child whose family erased her.
The question asks for what sin she was killed, exposing the absolute injustice of turning a dependent child's existence into family disgrace.
The Prophet is told not to admire wealth and children, for these apparent favors can become means of punishment; abundance is explicitly detached from honor.
Those who consume orphan property are described as eating fire, the judicial opposite of feeding and honoring the orphan.
The prohibition on killing children because of poverty is grounded in God's provision for parent and child; constriction cannot justify destroying the one needing care.
Fear of poverty must not lead to killing children, because God provides for them and their parents; expected restriction is no warrant for withheld life and care.
The Prophet must not drive away poor believers in pursuit of elite approval; vulnerable people may not be humiliated by a worldly rank calculation.
God tests some people through others until the privileged ask whether these are the ones God favored; the social encounter itself exposes their false scale of honor.
The Prophet must remain with devoted poor believers and not look past them toward worldly adornment, reversing attention based on visible provision.
Fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives, and crops are named as tests; it expands the harmful side of the section's two-sided ibtilā into concrete forms.
Believers are told they will be tested in property and persons, making ownership and loss arenas of patience rather than evidence of rank.
Israel's rescue from Pharaoh's slaughter is called a great بلاء from their Lord; deliverance and severe harm occupy one divinely governed ordeal.
The repeated Pharaoh-rescue scene again calls the ordeal بلاء من ربكم, relevant to the section's insistence that painful conditions remain within the Lord's trial.
Moses recalls rescue from Pharaoh's torment as containing a great trial from the Lord, tying remembered affliction to gratitude for deliverance.
Victory is described as بلاء حسنا from God; the root can name a favorable testing gift, not only suffering.
God makes some people a trial for others and asks whether they will be patient; differing human conditions test both the needy and those able to respond.
Every نعمة is said to come from God, and distress makes people cry to Him; it fixes the source of both the remembered ease and the appeal under restriction.
When distress is removed, some immediately associate others with their Lord, showing relief failing to mature into grateful recognition.
Their response is described as ingratitude for what God gave, making enjoyment a temporarily permitted test with consequences.
People rejoice when made to taste mercy and despair when harm follows their own deeds; the emotional swing parallels the two hasty verdicts in the section.
In adversity the human calls his Lord, but after نعمة he forgets the earlier dependence; changing conditions expose a failed memory of care.
Favor makes the human withdraw, while evil brings prolonged prayer; it completes the unstable relation to good and harm described at 41:49-50.
Mercy makes people rejoice and consequences make them ungrateful; the verse supplies another explicit reversal between reception and interpretation.
The human is introduced as anxiously constituted before 70:20-21 show panic under harm and withholding under good; it names the disposition behind both readings.
The human is intensely ungrateful to his Lord, supplying the moral diagnosis behind receiving nurture yet failing the dependent.
His intense love of wealth gives that ingratitude a material object and helps explain why received provision stops with him.
The slanderer amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, a concrete scene of possession becoming self-absorption rather than care.
He imagines his wealth has made him permanent, an extreme form of treating provision as a durable personal rank.
Wealth and children are the adornment of the nearer life, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord; possession and enduring worth are placed on different scales.
Worldly life is portrayed as adornment and rivalry in wealth and children that flourishes and then withers; the scene makes prosperous status visibly temporary.
People do not attain birr until they spend from what they love, making release of treasured provision the test of goodness.
Satan promises poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; anticipated restriction is identified as the pressure that can choke generosity.
Believers must spend from what God made them successors over, recasting ownership as temporary stewardship.
The covenant commands good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, and the poor; honoring the orphan belongs to a foundational social obligation.
Human development is traced through successive embryonic states, childhood, and maturity, a bodily instance of the section's dictionary definition of gradual nurture to completion.
Successive transformations culminate in another creation, giving concrete form to development حالا فحالا even though the رب root is not used in the ayah.
Creation proceeds from dust and embryo to child, maturity, and old age; the measured stages illuminate the section's account of Lordly upbringing.
وقد خلقكم أطوارا states that God created people in stages, a concise nonlexical parallel to the cited definition of رب as bringing a thing through states.
Moses defines the Lord as the One who gives each thing its form and then guides it, a divine answer to Pharaoh's claim of having raised him.
Abraham identifies his Lord as the One who created and guides him, beginning a sequence of sustaining acts that makes رب active care.
The Lord is the One who feeds and gives drink, placing provision within ongoing nurture rather than social honor.
Healing when ill extends Lordly care beyond abundance into bodily adversity.
Death and restored life complete Abraham's account of the Lord's governance through changing human states.
Guardians cast their pens to decide who will care for Mary; human competition is directed toward responsibility for a dependent child.
Moses' mother is told to nurse him and promised his return before exposing him to the river, joining maternal care, fear, and divine guardianship.
When Joseph reaches maturity God gives him judgment and knowledge; it completes the child-in-household scene of 12:21 with growth into adulthood.
Whoever seeks honor is told that all honor belongs to God and that good words and deeds rise, redirecting status from possessions to accountable action.
The slain believer wishes his people knew that his Lord forgave him and made him among the honored, locating genuine ikram beyond worldly standing.
The people of the garden receive fruits and are مكرمون; it is a true divine honor after judgment, unlike the provisional نعمة misread in the section.
وربك الأكرم names the Lord as most generous before 96:6-7 expose the human who sees himself self-sufficient; the sequence contrasts source and recipient.
فاستبقوا الخيرات commands people to outstrip one another in good deeds, a general Quranic form of the section's generosity-race dictionary sense.
Self-restrained poor people can be mistaken for rich and remain unrecognized; it specifies how need is overlooked and goodness reaches the dependent late.
The giver will finally be satisfied by his Lord, closing the passage in which taqwa and spending, rather than wealth retained, establish his standing.
After the garden's loss, its owners hope their Lord will replace it with better and turn their desire toward Him; failed provision becomes a chance to return.
